MD Driven

Prototype development and device troubleshooting for a medical device company in St. Louis.

Mechanical design

I’m designing a mechanical device from first concept through working prototype, modeling each iteration in SolidWorks and printing it on FDM printers. Each round is evaluated against the design requirements and reworked, including a redesign that simplified the concept considerably once testing showed the original approach would not work as intended.

The design involved adjustable geometry to accommodate variation between users.

Device reliability

I also troubleshoot the electrical and mechanical systems of the company’s medical device. That means working directly with the circuit boards: soldering connections, rewiring, and tracing faults back to their source.

Troubleshooting involves isolating each component on its own so a failure can be traced to its actual source instead of guessing at the system as a whole.

This work is proprietary and patent-pending, so it is described in general terms only. No designs, drawings or images are shown. I’m glad to discuss my process and engineering approach in an interview.

Accessible Xbox controller

A hardware fixture that lets a client with cerebral palsy use every button, including the ones on the back, from the front of the controller.

The need

We started by researching the motor limitations that come with cerebral palsy and identifying what makes a standard controller hard to use: limited fine motor control, and difficulty reaching the buttons and applying enough force. From those constraints we wrote design requirements around ergonomics, accessibility and ease of actuation.

We also talked with the client directly. She described how cerebral palsy affects her movement and which parts of play were hardest, so we could design around her instead of a generic user.

What I did

I contributed to the design and prototyping by helping develop and iterate on a physical attachment that modified the button layout and input mechanics. We rapidly modeled in SolidWorks, built, 3D-printed and tested prototypes, using her feedback and functional testing to refine the design inside tight time and resource limits.

The result

The final prototype reduced the precision and force each input takes. We enlarged the buttons and built a system that brings the rear buttons to the front of the controller, so everything is reachable without a wide range of motion or fine motor skills.

What I took from it

It strengthened my ability to apply design principles under tight time constraints, work with a multidisciplinary team, and build something with direct human impact.

Functional videos of the prototype are available on request.

Bulk Bag to Small Container

A system for astronauts to move loose particulate from a bulk bag into a small container, in a controlled amount, without adding single-use bags.

The problem

NASA needed a system that could transfer loose particulate from a larger bulk bag into a smaller container in a controlled fashion, to cut down on the small single-use bags carried into space.

The process

We followed a full engineering design cycle: problem definition and requirements analysis, then concept generation and evaluation of several approaches through iterative prototyping and testing, ending in a refined final solution. After a lot of brainstorming we landed on two related solutions, a bulk bag lid-mounted system and a simplified bulk bag system, plus a small container to receive the particulate. All of them use a seal we developed to keep the loose particulate under control.

We CAD modeled each idea in Fusion 360 to picture the final product and check early feasibility, then built initial prototypes and ran functional testing to find the limits of each design. Every round of testing fed the next iteration and moved us closer to our stated requirements.

The outcome

We shared design updates with NASA engineers throughout development. At the end of the year we presented the final design to a panel of NASA engineers and astronauts, which meant clearly communicating both our technical approach and our design trade-offs.

What I took from it

The project strengthened my skills in requirements definition, teamwork, iterative design, and turning technical work into a clear presentation. The full report documents the whole process, from the problem statement and brainstorming through the design requirements, decision matrix, testing results, feedback and reflection.

Engineered probiotic yeast

Over a year of research in probiotic engineering and targeted gut therapeutics, building a plasmid library in yeast that can secrete proteins of interest at a range of concentrations.

Saccharomyces boulardii is a resilient probiotic yeast that survives the changing temperature, pH and nutrients of the gut, which makes it a promising carrier for protein-based therapies. We transformed it with every combination of 5 promoters, 5 secretion signals and 5 terminators, creating a library of 125 unique strains, each expressing a reporter protein so secretion could be measured by luminescence.

I ran the in vitro luminescence assays to quantify secretion across strains and analyzed the data to identify statistically significant drivers of expression. I also assisted with the in vivo work in a mouse model, where we validated secretion through luminescence in stool samples.

125strains built and confirmed by colony PCR
1,800xexpression range across the library
28xgain in secreted anti-PD-1 binding activity

Promoter and secretion signal choice had the largest impact on expression, while terminators did not. Luminescence in mouse stool corresponded with the in vitro data, which suggests the strains stay functional in the gut and that lab results can predict in vivo performance.

Why it matters

This platform could treat a range of GI infections, diseases and cancers without invasive procedures. That potential to improve patients’ quality of life is what made the work worth doing, and it gave me experience in experimental design, data analysis and carrying bench results through to in vivo systems.

Wallace MJ, Kratschmer C, Brazil B, et al. “A combinatorial construct library enables an expanded expression range of secreted therapeutic proteins by probiotic yeast.” Trends in Biotechnology (2026).
